answer_text:
Assume \(n\) is an integer and we mean primes that are **exactly** of the form

\[
p=2n^2+1.
\]

Let

\[
\mathcal P=\{p\text{ prime}: p=2n^2+1\text{ for some }n\in\mathbb Z\}.
\]

The Dirichlet density is

\[
\delta(\mathcal P)
=
\lim_{s\to 1^+}
\frac{\sum_{p\in\mathcal P}p^{-s}}
{\sum_{p}p^{-s}},
\]

if the limit exists.

For \(s>1\),

\[
\sum_{p\in\mathcal P}p^{-s}
\le
\sum_{n=1}^\infty (2n^2+1)^{-s}
\le
\sum_{n=1}^\infty (2n^2)^{-s}
=
2^{-s}\zeta(2s).
\]

As \(s\to 1^+\),

\[
2^{-s}\zeta(2s)\to 2^{-1}\zeta(2)=\frac{\pi^2}{12},
\]

so the numerator is bounded near \(s=1\).

Meanwhile, the full prime sum diverges as \(s\to1^+\); in fact

\[
\sum_{p}p^{-s}\sim \log\frac{1}{s-1}\to\infty.
\]

Therefore,

\[
0\le
\frac{\sum_{p\in\mathcal P}p^{-s}}
{\sum_{p}p^{-s}}
\le
\frac{C}{\sum_{p}p^{-s}}
\to 0.
\]

Hence the Dirichlet density is

\[
\boxed{0}.
\]

Equivalently, up to \(X\) there are at most \(\sqrt{X/2}\) such primes, while the total number of primes up to \(X\) is \(\sim X/\log X\), so the natural density is also \(0\).
